concepts.title: Principles
concepts.description: - **Cloud is built on the Local core.
concepts.body:
- **Cloud is built on the Local core.** Everything that is not storage lives
  once, in `packages/core`: `format.ts` (pure: the OKF text format, ids and
  their canonical form, link extraction and retargeting, snippets, statuses,
  frontmatter construction, the weeding rules, the status counts, the graph
  walk) and `library.ts` (pure: thesaurus, query expansion, finding aids,
  shelves). Both are free of `node:*` imports, so the Convex runtime imports
  them as `@librocat/core/format` and `@librocat/core/library`. Local wraps
  them around files and Orama (`okf.ts`, `memindex.ts`, `service.ts`); Cloud
  wraps them around Convex rows (`apps/web/convex/model.ts`). What stays
  per tier is storage: files vs rows, Git log vs the revisions table, the
  Orama ranking vs the Convex search index, and Cloud's quotas, credits, and
  circulation. `packages/core/tests/format.test.ts` is the contract both
  tiers inherit. A new pure rule goes into `format.ts`, never into
  `model.ts`.
- **OKF is the format; the index is derived and rebuildable.** Local's
  source of truth is the user's Git repo; Cloud's is the workspace, exported
  as the same OKF files; `librocat pull` writes them into a Git repo.
- **The MCP is the only full read/write interface.** The dashboard manages the
  system (billing, connected agents, the team, export/delete) and browses
  read-only.
- **No database locally.** The Local index lives in memory, rebuilt from the
  files at launch. Rebuilds take milliseconds at local scale.
- **Stateless remote MCP, OAuth 2.1.** Every request carries the agent's
  access token (Better Auth on Convex is the authorization server,
  `apps/web/convex/auth.ts`); the route verifies it (mcp-handler
  `withMcpAuth`), Convex verifies it again, and every Convex function
  resolves the workspace from the user it names. No session state, no API
  tokens.

concepts.title: Search
concepts.description: - Local: Orama (pure TypeScript, bm25).
concepts.body:
- Local: Orama (pure TypeScript, bm25). The schema indexes title, description,
  body, tags, and type. Filters (`type`, `tag`, `status`) apply after ranking.
- Cloud: a Convex search index over one concatenated `searchText` field on the
  `bodies` table (body + search text live apart from the catalog record, so
  the metadata paths stay small), with `workspaceId`, `type`, and `status`
  as filter fields.

Both expand the query through the tag thesaurus first (`@librocat/core/library`,
the one core module Cloud imports — it must stay free of `node:fs`), map a
`tag` facet through it, and sink deprecated hits below live ones unless
`status` is filtered. Both return the same result shape, with a bracketed
`[match]` snippet on the reader's own words.

concepts.title: Stack
concepts.description: | Piece | Service | |-------|---------| | Remote MCP endpoint | Next.
concepts.body:
| Piece | Service |
|-------|---------|
| Remote MCP endpoint | Next.js route on Vercel (`/mcp`): [mcp-handler](https://github.com/vercel/mcp-handler) 2.x over the official MCP SDK v2 |
| Database + functions + scheduled indexation | Convex |
| Auth | Better Auth on Convex (`@convex-dev/better-auth`): email + password with emailed codes for the dashboard, and the OAuth 2.1 authorization server for the MCP |
| Dashboard + landing | Next.js on Vercel (shadcn/ui) |
| Billing | Stripe Checkout + a Billing Meter for pay-as-you-go index credits |
| Automatic indexation | Vercel AI Gateway: Jev (`typesafe-ai/jev`, typed judgments) first, `google/gemini-3.8-flash` for what Jev cannot fill (paid plans) |

concepts.title: How the remote MCP works
concepts.description: - The endpoint is `https://librocat.
concepts.body:
- The endpoint is `https://librocat.dev/mcp` (in development
  `http://localhost:3000/mcp`). It speaks stateless Streamable HTTP: the
  2026-07-28 MCP revision natively, and 2025-era clients through the SDK's
  stateless fallback. GET/DELETE session calls answer 405 by design.
- Clients authenticate with OAuth 2.1, the way remote MCP servers such as
  Stripe's, Vercel's, and Resend's do: no header to configure, no token to
  copy. A call without a token gets a 401 whose `WWW-Authenticate` names the
  protected-resource metadata (`/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp`),
  which names the authorization server (`https://librocat.dev/api/auth`).
  The agent registers itself (dynamic client registration), opens the
  browser for the user to sign in and approve it on `/consent`, and comes
  back with a one-hour JWT access token bound to `https://librocat.dev/mcp`
  plus a refresh token.
- The route verifies the token against Better Auth's JWKS, registers the
  same tool table as the Local server (`packages/mcp/src/tools.ts`) over a
  Convex backend (`apps/web/src/lib/mcp-backend.ts`), and calls each Convex
  function in `apps/web/convex/mcp.ts` with that same token. Convex checks it
  again (`convex/auth.config.ts`), resolves the workspace from the user it
  names, and checks the agent still holds the user's grant, so a disconnect
  on the dashboard takes effect on the agent's next call.
- Tools: the same surface as Local, minus `ingest_repo` and `reindex` (there
  is no filesystem on this endpoint) — fifteen tools. See
  [mcp-tools.md](./mcp-tools.md). Concept bodies are capped at 64 KB.
- Concepts live in a Convex table with a search index. Links live in a second
  table, so `neighbors` and `graph` stay indexed queries. Revisions live in a
  third: every `ingest`, `update`, `rename`, and automatic indexation appends
  a full snapshot, so `history` is the workspace's commit log and any past
  revision is readable. Cloud needs no Git repo; export the OKF zip when you
  want the files in one.

concepts.title: Two ways to reach it: directly, or through the librocat CLI
concepts.description: Everything above describes the endpoint itself: any MCP client that speaks remote MCP connects to `https://librocat.
concepts.body:
Everything above describes the endpoint itself: any MCP client that speaks
remote MCP connects to `https://librocat.dev/mcp` and runs the OAuth sign-in
(the Agent Plugin's `mcp.json` is exactly that URL).

For an agent that can only spawn stdio servers, `librocat mcp --remote`
(the npm package) bridges stdio to this endpoint over the official MCP
client SDK (`packages/mcp/src/remote-backend.ts`), signed in with `librocat
login` (`packages/mcp/src/oauth.ts`). It registers the exact tool table
above, plus `ingest_repo` (it has a filesystem, so it reads a repo on your
disk and writes the result here) and `reindex` as a documented no-op, so its
tool list matches the local server's seventeen. See
[docs/local.md §Local and hosted, together](./local.md#local-and-hosted-together).

concepts.title: Auth: OAuth 2.1, one identity for both doors
concepts.description: Better Auth runs inside the Convex deployment (`convex/auth.
concepts.body:
Better Auth runs inside the Convex deployment (`convex/auth.ts`, installed
locally under `convex/betterAuth` because the OAuth provider adds tables).
The same user signs in to the dashboard and approves agents; a write through
the MCP records both (`revisions.userId`, `revisions.client`). Next.js
proxies `/api/auth/*` to the Convex site (`src/lib/auth-server.ts`) and
serves the discovery documents at the site root (`src/app/.well-known`).

- Access tokens: RS256 JWTs, `iss` = `SITE_URL/api/auth`, `aud` =
  `SITE_URL/mcp`, one hour. Refresh tokens rotate on use.
- Connected agents: the Connect page lists every agent the user approved
  (`convex/agents.ts`) and disconnects one immediately.
- Teams: each person has their own account; an admin shares an invite link
  (`convex/team.ts`, `/invite/[code]`), up to 10 seats on Team.
- Not built yet: client ID metadata documents (the MCP 2026-07-28
  preference over dynamic registration) wait for `@convex-dev/better-auth`
  to support Better Auth 1.7 (`@better-auth/cimd`).

concepts.title: Automatic indexation and index credits
concepts.description: What hosted does that a local library leaves to your agent.
concepts.body:
What hosted does that a local library leaves to your agent. After an
`ingest` or `update` that leaves a concept **without a description or without
tags**, a scheduled Convex action (`convex/indexation.ts`) catalogs it, in
the cheapest stage that can do the job:

1. It reserves one **index credit** in a mutation (atomic).
2. **Code** builds the candidates: up to eight prose sentences from the body
   (5 to 40 words each) for the description, and up to 40 tags from the
   library's vocabulary (tags used on the concept's shelf first, then the
   rest, then the thesaurus's unused preferred tags). Each tag carries its
   scope note and up to three titles already filed under it, the shelf list
   a cataloger checks before choosing a heading.
3. **Jev** (`typesafe-ai/jev` through the AI Gateway's `/v1/evaluate`,
   override with `LIBROCAT_EVAL_MODEL`) answers typed questions in one
   request: which candidate sentence works as the description (or none), and
   one yes/no per candidate tag, judged against its scope note and shelf
   list. Jev selects; it never writes text, so a transcribed description
   cannot invent a fact. Its input costs $0.042 per million tokens and its
   output is free, a small fraction of a generative call; each call's real
   cost is in the log line below.
4. **Gemini**, on Individual and Team only: whatever Jev could not fill goes
   to `google/gemini-3.8-flash` (override with `LIBROCAT_AI_MODEL`), which
   writes a one-sentence description or tags, told the existing vocabulary
   so it reuses terms instead of coining synonyms. **Then Jev checks it**:
   the description is kept only when Jev finds everything it says in the
   concept (probability 0.8 or more), and each tag only when Jev finds it a
   subject of the concept (0.6 or more). If Jev cannot be reached, nothing
   Gemini wrote is kept. On Free the blank stays for the writing agent.
5. It writes only what the writer left blank, files under the most specific
   tag (a broader tag goes when a narrower one is there, Cutter's rule of
   specific entry), records how in `cataloged` (`description: transcribed |
   generated`, `tags: selected | generated`, `by`, `at`), and stamps
   `indexed_at`. When nothing could be filled, the credit is refunded. The
   log line `{"indexation":{"jev":…,"generated":…,"verified":…}}` records each
   stage and its cost.

Gemini and Libro's sessions ask the gateway for zero data retention
(`providerOptions.gateway.zeroDataRetention`). Jev cannot: the gateway lists
no zero-retention provider for it (`"zdr": "none"` in
`https://ai-gateway.vercel.sh/v1/models`) and refuses such a request with a
400. Every default model is listed `"no_training": "all"`.

Credits per calendar month (UTC): Free 500, Individual 500, Team 2,500
(`INDEX_CREDITS` in `convex/model.ts`). Past the included credits, a paid
workspace continues only when it turned **pay-as-you-go** on in Billing:
$0.01 per extra concept (`INDEX_CREDIT_OVERAGE_CENTS`), reported to a Stripe
Billing Meter per concept. Otherwise indexation pauses until next month.
`status` reports `index_credits` (`included`, `used`, `remaining`, `overage`,
`pay_as_you_go`, `period`); the Overview shows the bar; Billing has the
switch. Agents that already catalog fully (the okf-authoring skill) spend
nothing.

Env on the Convex deployment: `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY`, optional
`LIBROCAT_EVAL_MODEL`, `LIBROCAT_AI_MODEL`, `LIBROCAT_AI_GATEWAY_URL`.

concepts.title: Libro, the library cat
concepts.description: librocat's librarian is a library cat named Libro.
concepts.body:
librocat's librarian is a library cat named Libro. In the hosted library,
Libro is the automated work on a library that people and agents should not
have to do:

- **Automatic cataloging** (index credits, above): Libro fills a missing
  description or tags after `ingest`/`update`.
- **The review shelf** (`convex/libro.ts`, table `proposals`): once a week
  (cron, Monday 07:00 UTC) or on "Ask Libro now" (Overview), Libro reads
  the library and files proposals: *supersede* (two concepts with the same
  title, or the same name on two shelves; the older is superseded by the
  newer), *retire* (a stable concept that already carries `superseded_by`,
  or one never read in 90 days), *merge tag* (two spellings of one tag; the
  rarer becomes a `use_for` of the common one in the thesaurus). Libro
  proposes, the user disposes: Approve applies the change as a revision
  `by: "libro"`, Dismiss files it away for good (one proposal per kind,
  subject, target, ever). `status` reports `review_shelf`, the open count.
  *Past its date*: a live concept whose OKF `stale_after` has passed. **Still
  true** records the person's check (OKF `verified`, `human:<id>`) and moves
  the date 90 days ahead; **Retire** deprecates it. The date is part of the
  proposal's key, so a concept comes back when its new date passes.
  Every plan gets this mechanical pass; it calls no model. On Free the
  weekly pass runs when something was written since the last one, and
  monthly while the library sits idle, so an idle library costs nothing.
- **Jev's screens, every plan**, after every review, when the deployment
  has `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY`. No generative model; a fraction of a cent a
  run.
  - **Review dates** (`libro.datesScreen`): Jev reads what changed since it
    last looked. For anything tied to a date, a version, a price, or a
    person, a *Review date* proposal: set it, or dismiss it.
  - **Concept embeddings** (`convex/similar.ts`): each concept (title,
    description, the first 2,000 characters of the body) is embedded by the
    model the reference desk uses.
    - One 256-dimension vector per concept, in `conceptVectors` (vector
      index).
    - Embedded again when the concept changes, and deleted with it.
    - At most 512 concepts a run; a bigger library continues in the next
      run.
  - **Duplicates by meaning:** each concept embedded in the run looks up
    its four nearest.
    - Pairs at cosine 0.75 or more that don't share a title go to Jev: up
      to 20, with the eve screen's "same subject?" question.
    - Confirmed pairs go on the shelf as supersede proposals.
  - **No answer:** the questions agents asked in the last 30 days and found
    no answer to (up to 10, most asked first) are embedded as queries.
    - Up to three concepts per question, at cosine 0.45 or more and
      written before the question was last asked, go to Jev: "is this
      concept about what was asked?"
    - At 0.8 or more, a `gap` proposal. **Mark stale** sets the concept's
      `stale_after` to today, so every read says `stale: true` until
      someone verifies or updates it.
    - **Dismiss** is for good: one per concept and question, ever.
  - **Failures:** when a call fails, nothing is marked done, and the next
    review retries.
  - **Checking the live model:** `npx convex run embeddings:probe`.
- **Libro proper, the eve agent** (`agents/libro`, Vercel eve), Individual
  and Team only: when the deployment knows where Libro lives (`LIBRO_URL` +
  `LIBRO_SECRET` on Convex), every review also summons an eve session for the
  workspace, one Libro credit each (`LIBRO_CREDITS`: 20/mo on Individual,
  100/mo on Team, then $0.10 a run with pay-as-you-go). **Jev screens
  first**: code pairs concepts on one shelf that share two or more tags or
  most of a title, and Jev judges up to 20 pairs ("the same subject?") in
  one request. Pairs it confirms go on the shelf as supersede proposals and
  into the session's brief. When nothing is confirmed and nothing

concepts.title: The reference desk and Libro's weekly report
concepts.description: **The ready-reference file** (`convex/reference.
concepts.body:
**The ready-reference file** (`convex/reference.ts`). Every MCP `search` is
a question put to the library, so `search` is a mutation that files it:

- **What is kept:** the query (capped at 300 characters), how many results
  it found and the first five ids, and who asked (the person and the
  agent).
- **The answer:** the first of those results the same asker opens within
  ten minutes (`get_concept`).
- **Secrets:** a query that looks like it carries one is never kept.
- **Retention:** questions are kept 90 days (a daily cron prunes them) and
  go with the index when it is deleted.

In the background (`fileQuestion`, when the deployment has
`AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY`):

- **Grouping by meaning.** The question is embedded
  (`convex/embeddings.ts`): Qwen3-Embedding-8B
  (`alibaba/qwen3-embedding-8b`, open weights), pinned to DeepInfra, which
  runs it in the US, and every request requires zero data retention.
  - The embedding only proposes: the three nearest earlier questions
    (cosine 0.5 or more).
  - Jev decides whether the new question asks one of them again
    (probability 0.8 or more). If it does, the question takes that
    question's key, so rewordings count as one question.
  - Its own key stays on it as `fold`, a "see" reference. The same words
    asked again get the earlier answer with no new embedding.
  - One 256-dimension vector is kept per distinct question
    (`questionClusters`, vector index).
  - Without a key, or without Jev's judgment, questions group by their
    content words.
- **Was it answered?** Search matches any word, so "found something" is not
  "found an answer". In the same Jev request, Jev judges whether one of the
  first three results answers the question. A question is unanswered when
  it found nothing, or nothing Jev judged an answer.

What it gives back:

- **Ready reference:** a question asked again gets the concept that
  answered it before as the first hit, marked `ready_reference: true`. A
  rewording filed under it gets the same.
- **The reference desk** on the Overview: the last 30 days, split into
  "Asked most" (and what answered each) and "No answer yet": the gaps in
  the collection, what to write down next.
- **The concepts behind the gaps:** after each review, the concepts an
  unanswered question is about go on the review shelf, to mark stale
  (above).

**Libro's weekly report** (`convex/report.ts`):

- **What it covers:** what arrived and changed this week, what is past its
  review date, what waits on the review shelf, what agents read, and the
  questions that found no answer.
- **Where it appears:** live on the Overview, and every Monday at 08:00 UTC
  by email (Resend), an hour after Libro's review.
- **Who gets the email:** admins by default. Each member turns it on or off
  on the Overview.
- **Unsubscribing:** every email carries a one-click unsubscribe (RFC 8058
  `List-Unsubscribe`) that needs no sign-in: `/api/unsubscribe`, with an
  HMAC of the member's id signed with `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET`.
- **Empty libraries** get no email.

concepts.title: Projects are shelves, not libraries
concepts.description: One workspace is one library: one thesaurus, one graph, one weeding report, one review shelf for Libro.
concepts.body:
One workspace is one library: one thesaurus, one graph, one weeding report,
one review shelf for Libro. Projects live on **shelves**, the leading
directory of the concept id (`acme/…`, `billing/…`). `search` and `list`
take `shelf` to scope a read to one project; an agent working in that
project reads its shelf first and the whole library second, so a decision
made in one project is still found from another. Every shelf gets a finding
aid. Make a second library only when access must differ (a client under
NDA, personal vs employer), never to get a per-project view.

concepts.title: Several libraries
concepts.description: A person can belong to several libraries, like Supabase projects: their own, and the teams they joined.
concepts.body:
A person can belong to several libraries, like Supabase projects: their own,
and the teams they joined. Each library has its own members, plan, quota,
review shelf, and address for agents. Supabase's MCP takes the project in
its URL (`?project_ref=`), and so does librocat's:

- `https://librocat.dev/mcp` reaches your **default** library, the first
  you joined. Every installed config keeps working, and an agent never
  changes library by itself.
- `https://librocat.dev/mcp?library=<slug>` reaches another one. A repo pins
  its library with this URL in its `.mcp.json`. The dashboard's Library
  settings and Connect pages show each library's URL. The CLI takes
  `--library <slug>` (or `LIBROCAT_LIBRARY`).
- One OAuth sign-in covers all of them. The library travels on the MCP URL,
  never in the token: the token's audience stays `/mcp` (a resource has no
  query, RFC 9728; the `/api/auth` proxy drops one a client sends), and
  every call checks membership (`convex/mcp.ts`, `convex/membership.ts`). A
  library you don't belong to answers "no library", never a fallback.
- The dashboard shows one library at a time (the switcher at the top of the
  sidebar). Switching changes the dashboard only; agents keep the library
  their URL names.
- **New library** makes one on the Free plan. A person can own two Free
  libraries (`FREE_LIBRARIES` in `convex/model.ts`); a paid one never counts.
  **Delete library** (its owner) removes it and everything in it and cancels
  its plan. Deleting an account deletes every library its person owns.
- Joining a team through an invite folds away your own library only if it is
  empty and has no plan, so the team's becomes your default; one holding
  knowledge stays, and the team's is reached by its slug.

concepts.title: Plans and quota
concepts.description: Account memory is measured in **concepts**, never in bytes.
concepts.body:
Account memory is measured in **concepts**, never in bytes.

- Free: every new account. 1 user, 1,000 concepts, 500 index credits/mo
  (Jev only, no Gemini), the mechanical review shelf, no Libro sessions, no
  pay-as-you-go. No card.
- Individual ($12/mo, or $10/mo billed yearly): 1 user, 5,000 concepts, 500
  index credits/mo, 20 Libro sessions/mo, then pay as you go.
- Team ($60/mo, or $50/mo billed yearly): up to 10 users, 15,000 concepts,
  2,500 index credits/mo, 100 Libro sessions/mo, then pay as you go. Each
  person signs in with their own account and joins through an invite link
  (Team page).
- Both paid plans check out through Stripe (one price per plan per
  interval: `STRIPE_PRICE_ID_INDIVIDUAL`, `STRIPE_PRICE_ID_TEAM`,
  `STRIPE_PRICE_ID_INDIVIDUAL_ANNUAL`, `STRIPE_PRICE_ID_TEAM_ANNUAL`, plus
  the metered `STRIPE_PRICE_ID_INDEXATION` on every paid subscription).
  When a subscription ends, the workspace returns to Free and keeps every
  concept; new ones wait until it is under the Free limit.
- The `ingest` mutation enforces the quota. Overwrites of existing concepts
  always pass.
- Every write is checked for secrets first (`assertNoSecrets` in
  `packages/core/src/format.ts`: private keys and the key formats of AWS,
  GitHub, Stripe, Anthropic, OpenAI, Slack, Google, and npm). A match is
  refused with a pointer to record where the secret lives instead.
- Self-hosting: `LIBROCAT_SELF_HOST=1` on the Convex deployment lifts every
  limit, and on the Next.js app it hides Billing and the plan bars. Without
  the flag the plan limits apply, so a hosted deployment never falls open by
  accident. `self-host/` runs the whole service with Docker Compose on a
  self-hosted Convex, with the flag set ([SELF_HOSTING.md](../SELF_HOSTING.md)).

concepts.title: Your data: export and delete
concepts.description: The dashboard Overview has two controls (the control plane, not the editor): - **Export index** downloads the workspace as a plain OKF zip, with a finding aid (`index.
concepts.body:
The dashboard Overview has two controls (the control plane, not the editor):

- **Export index** downloads the workspace as a plain OKF zip, with a
  finding aid (`index.md`) per directory. The unzipped `okf/` directory drops
  into the free Local tool (`LIBROCAT_BUNDLE=./okf`).
- **Delete index** erases every concept, link, and revision after a
  confirmation. (`delete` in the MCP weeds one concept the same way.)

The entrance is as open as the exit: `librocat push [dir]` (the CLI in
`librocat`, once logged in) reads a local OKF bundle and writes every
concept into the logged-in workspace, so upgrading from Local does not mean
starting from an empty library.

Data gravity is the moat — lock-in is not. The exit door stays open on purpose.

concepts.title: Local development
concepts.description: The Convex project is `librocat` (team `<your-team>`, managed through the Vercel marketplace).
concepts.body:
The Convex project is `librocat` (team `<your-team>`, managed through
the Vercel marketplace). `pnpm exec convex dev` gives every logged-in developer
their own dev deployment of it and writes `NEXT_PUBLIC_CONVEX_URL` to
`apps/web/.env.local`:

```bash
cd apps/web
pnpm exec convex login                            # once per machine
pnpm exec convex dev                              # your dev deployment, keeps running
pnpm exec convex env set SITE_URL http://localhost:3000   # once per deployment
pnpm exec convex env set BETTER_AUTH_SECRET "$(openssl rand -base64 32)"
pnpm exec convex env set LIBROCAT_E2E 1                  # dev only: the e2e fixtures below
pnpm run dev                                      # dashboard + /mcp on :3000
```

Without a Convex account, `CONVEX_AGENT_MODE=anonymous pnpm exec convex dev`
runs a local Convex on :3210 instead; the rest is the same.

Signing up in the dashboard sends a verification code through Resend. With no
`AUTH_RESEND_KEY` on the deployment, set `AUTH_DEV_LOG_CODES=1`
(`pnpm exec convex env set AUTH_DEV_LOG_CODES 1`) and the code is written to
the Convex log instead (`pnpm exec convex logs`). Never set it on prod.

Then, with an access token signed for a fixture user (what an agent gets from
the OAuth flow, minus the browser):

```bash
LIBROCAT_MCP_TOKEN=$(pnpm exec convex run dev:issueTestAccessToken '{"plan":"individual"}' | jq -r .token) \
LIBROCAT_MCP_URL=http://localhost:3000/mcp pnpm test                              # remote MCP e2e
LIBROCAT_MCP_URL=http://localhost:3000/mcp LIBROCAT_E2E_CLI_CWD=. pnpm test         # the whole OAuth flow
LIBROCAT_E2E_CONVEX_URL=https://<your-dev>.convex.cloud pnpm test               # dashboard functions (or http://127.0.0.1:3210)
```

To exercise automatic indexation and Jev without an AI Gateway key, start the
fake gateway (`node tests/fake-gateway.ts`: chat completions and
`/v1/evaluate`), point the local deployment at it (`pnpm exec convex env set
AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY test` and `pnpm exec convex env set LIBROCAT_AI_GATEWAY_URL
http://127.0.0.1:8787/v1`), and run the MCP e2e with `LIBROCAT_FAKE_GATEWAY=1`
(and `tests/libro.e2e.test.ts` with `LIBROCAT_FAKE_EVE=1` too, for Libro's
screen). Unset the key again before the dashboard e2e, which expects no

To exercise Libro's credit/overage path without a real eve deploy, start the
fake eve (`node tests/fake-eve.ts`), point the local deployment at it
(`pnpm exec convex env set LIBRO_URL http://127.0.0.1:8788` and `pnpm exec convex
env set LIBRO_SECRET test`), and run the dashboard e2e with
`LIBROCAT_FAKE_EVE=1`. This one needs the CLI (`runNow`'s dev-only setup and
the mid-test `LIBRO_URL` flip) to administer the *same* deployment the test

(`http://127.0.0.1:3210`), the one this path is meant to run against.
Pointed anywhere else instead (a scratch directory with its own local
backend, say), set `LIBROCAT_E2E_CLI_CWD` to that directory.

Production: the Vercel project `librocat` builds `apps/web` and runs `convex

concepts.title: Cutter's objects of the catalog
concepts.description: Cutter says a catalog exists to do three things.
concepts.body:
Cutter says a catalog exists to do three things. Here is how librocat does
each.

| Object (Cutter) | In librocat | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Find a book whose **title** or **subject** is known | `search` (title, description, body, tags), expanded through the thesaurus; `get_concept` by id | Met |
| Find a book whose **author** is known | `search`/`list` with `author`: a person (a member's email, or a Git author in Local), `me`, or an agent by name; `get_concept` lists a concept's `authors` | Met (2026-09-26) |
| Show what the library has **on a subject** | `list`/`search` with `tag`, which now includes the tag's narrower terms; `thesaurus` shows the headings | Met, improved here |
| Show what the library has **in a kind** of literature | `list`/`search` with `type` (Decision, Runbook, ...) and `shelf`; finding aids per directory | Met |
| Help **choose** between books (edition, character) | The one-line `description`, `status` (draft, stable, deprecated), `superseded_by`, revisions, and now `cataloged` (how the record was made) | Met, improved here |

concepts.title: Validated: what librocat already does the way the books say
concepts.description: - **Controlled vocabulary.
concepts.body:
- **Controlled vocabulary.** Dana warns that «Domestic animals», «Farm
  animals», and «Animals, domestic» for one subject "scatter the
  references". His cure is a printed list of headings, checked every time.
  librocat's thesaurus, the synonym folding on write (`use_for`), and Libro's
  "merge tag" proposals are that cure, applied automatically.
- **Cross-references.** Dana's cross-reference cards send a reader from
  "pigs" to "swine" (see) and on to "domestic animals" (see also). librocat
  has `use_for` for the first and `broader`/`narrower` for the second.
- **Classify for the reader.** Dana: when unsure, file a book where its
  readers will look for it. Jev's tag question asks exactly that: should the
  concept be filed under the tag "so that someone browsing that tag finds
  it"?
- **The shelf list and the call number.** Dana's shelf list, a catalog in
  shelf order, is librocat's finding aid (`finding_aid`, `index.md` per
  directory). His call number is the concept id: it says where the concept
  stands and tells it apart from its neighbors.
- **Accessioning.** Dana calls the accession book "a life history of every
  book". librocat keeps one: every write is a revision with who, when, and
  which agent.
- **Use is the test.** Dana: "no useless lumber is more useless than unused
  books." A hosted library counts retrievals (circulation), and
  `weed_report` lists what nobody reads.
- **Inventory.** Dana's periodic check of the library for what is missing or
  out of place is `status` (link health) and `weed_report` (broken links,
  orphans).
- **Selection fits the users.** Dana's chapter on choosing books is the
  `collection-policy` skill: what belongs in this library, and for whom.

concepts.title: Improved in this change
concepts.body:
1. **Scope notes** (ANSI/NISO Z39.19 "SN"). Dana says the list of headings
   must be "marked and annotated to fit your special needs". A thesaurus
   term now carries a `scope_note`: what the tag covers, and what belongs
   elsewhere. Hosted cataloging reads it when it chooses tags.
2. **Related terms** (Z39.19 "RT"). Cutter's syndetic catalog also refers
   to "illustrative and coördinate subjects", the "see also" that is neither
   broader nor narrower. A term now has `related`.
3. **A tag filter includes narrower terms.** Cutter's references run from a
   subject down to the subjects under it. `list` and `search` with a `tag`
   now include every narrower term (at any depth), so asking for «auth»
   finds what is filed under «oauth». Both engines, one function
   (`tagFacet`).
4. **Specific entry** (Cutter, rule 93: "Enter a work under its
   subject-heading, not under the heading of a class which includes that
   subject"). Hosted cataloging drops a broader tag when a narrower one
   applies (`specificEntry`).
5. **Check the shelf list before choosing a heading.** Dana: before placing
   a book in a class, "examine your shelf-list and see that the books
   already there are of like nature with it". Jev's tag questions now carry,
   for each candidate tag, its scope note and titles already filed under
   it.
6. **Transcribe; bracket what you supply.** Cutter asks that the title be
   "copied ... exactly" and that information the cataloger supplies be
   marked (in brackets). librocat's description is preferably a sentence
   transcribed from the concept, selected by Jev, not written. When a model
   writes one instead (paid plans), Jev checks it against the concept and it
   is kept only when supported. Either way, the concept records how, in
   `cataloged` (`description: transcribed | generated`, `tags: selected |
   generated`, `by`, `at`). The entry goes as soon as a writer changes the
   field.
7. **Libro's merge drafts are checked.** A merge draft is model-written, so
   Jev checks it against its two sources and the review shelf shows the
   result. A draft that invents is flagged before anyone approves it.
8. **Review dates, and a loop that keeps the library current.** OKF's
   `stale_after` marks when a concept should be checked again, and agents
   can now set it on `ingest` and `update`. Every search hit says `stale:
   true` once the date passes, `weed_report` lists it (MUSTIE's
   "misleading", made mechanical), and Libro puts it on the review shelf.
   **Still true** records who checked it (OKF `verified`) and moves the date
   a cycle ahead; **Retire** deprecates it. Agents can verify too (`update`
   with `verify: true`).

concepts.title: How the cataloging pipeline avoids hallucination
concepts.description: Automatic cataloging (hosted, `apps/web/convex/indexation.
concepts.body:
Automatic cataloging (hosted, `apps/web/convex/indexation.ts`) is built so a
catalog record cannot say something the concept does not:

1. **Select before generating.** Code gathers candidates (the concept's own
   sentences, the library's own tags). Jev, a small judgment model, picks
   among them. Selection cannot invent a fact, and it is the cheapest stage
   ($0.042 per million input tokens, output free).
2. **Generate only what selection could not fill**, on paid plans only, and
   tell the model the existing vocabulary.
3. **Verify what was generated.** A second Jev request asks whether the
   concept states everything the description says (kept at 0.8 or more) and
   whether each tag is a subject of the concept (0.6 or more). What fails is
   dropped and left for the writing agent. If Jev cannot be asked, nothing
   generated is kept.
4. **Never overwrite a writer**, and **record provenance** (`cataloged`), so
   a reader can tell a transcribed description from a generated one.
5. **A person decides on the shelf.** Libro proposes; nothing on the review
   shelf changes until someone approves it, and every approval is a
   revision.

concepts.title: Libro's job: keep the library current, and say what it shows
concepts.description: Libro, the library cat, is the librarian of a managed library, and its first duty is the one Dana gives the whole profession: a library is only as good as its use, and stale books are "useless lumber".
concepts.body:
Libro, the library cat, is the librarian of a managed library, and its first
duty is the one Dana gives the whole profession: a library is only as good
as its use, and stale books are "useless lumber". Libro's work, in the order
it happens:

1. **Catalog on arrival.** Every concept gets a record (description, tags),
   selected from its own words and the library's vocabulary.
2. **Keep it current.** Flag what may be outdated: past its review date,
   never read, superseded but still marked stable, duplicated. Propose; a
   person decides, and the decision is recorded.
3. **Keep it consistent.** Fold synonyms, fix links on renames, draft merges
   for duplicates, and have every draft checked against its sources.
4. **Report.** Tell the team what the library shows: what arrived, what is
   stale, what agents read most, and what they asked for and did not find.

Libro cannot see the world change, so staleness needs signals. Today:
review dates (`stale_after`), circulation, supersession, duplicates, and,
since 2026-09-26, time-bound claims: after each review, Jev reads what was
written or changed since it last looked, and for anything tied to a date,
a version, a price, or a person, Libro suggests a review date on the shelf
(a month to a year out, as Jev judges). A person sets it or dismisses it.
And, also since 2026-09-26, the code itself: a concept names the files it
describes (OKF `sources`), and when a commit touches one, `changed` sets
its review date to now and Libro puts it on the shelf with the file and
the commit. And, since 2026-09-27, the questions agents asked and found no
answer to (the ready-reference file, below). Each is embedded as a question
to look up. The concepts nearest to it, written before it was last asked,
are where its answer should have been. Jev judges whether each is about
what was asked, and Libro puts the ones it is sure of on the shelf:
**Mark stale** sets the review date to today, so the concept reads as
stale until someone checks it, and **Dismiss** is for good.

concepts.title: The ready-reference file, and Libro's report (built 2026-09-25)
concepts.description: Dana, ch.
concepts.body:
Dana, ch. XIII: "Many questions come up again and again. Of these, and of
the references which answered them, notes should be kept." librocat keeps
that file (`convex/reference.ts`):

- Every question an agent asks the library (a `search`) is filed, with what
  it found and the concept the agent opened next: its answer.
- Asked again, the question gets its answer first (`ready_reference`).
- Rewordings of one question are grouped by embedding, and only when Jev
  judges that they ask the same thing.
- Jev judges whether the results really answered the question. The ones
  that did not are the collection's gaps, the librarian's cue for what to
  write down next.

Libro reports what the file and the library show every Monday, on the
Overview and by email (`convex/report.ts`): the library's annual report,
weekly.

concepts.title: Accession numbers are never reused (built 2026-09-26)
concepts.description: Dana, ch.
concepts.body:
Dana, ch. XIX: an accession number, once given, is never given again. A
deleted concept's id could otherwise be taken by a new concept with a
different meaning, and links or agents that remembered the old one would
reach the new one. So a deleted id, and the old id of a renamed concept,
are retired: a derived id never takes one again, reading one says what
became of it (deleted on a date, or renamed to what), and an explicit id
that takes one says so. Local keeps them in the bundle's `log.md`, OKF's
update log; hosted keeps them per workspace and exports the same file.

concepts.title: Lists of additions (built 2026-09-27)
concepts.description: Dana, ch.
concepts.body:
Dana, ch. XXV: "Print lists of additions." The root finding aid, the
library's front page (`index.md`), opens with what arrived in the last seven
days, newest first. Hosted, that comes from each concept's creation; Local,
from Git (the commit that added the file, or now for one not committed yet).
Agents read it with `finding_aid`, and the hosted export carries it.

concepts.title: Embeddings: what they are for here, and which model (2026-09-25, updated 2026-09-26)
concepts.description: **Where embeddings are used:** as a candidate generator, never a judge.
concepts.body:
**Where embeddings are used:** as a candidate generator, never a judge.
Jev judges everything they propose. Three jobs, all hosted:
- grouping rewordings of a question in the ready-reference file, where
  there is no vocabulary to control (2026-09-25);
- Libro's duplicates by meaning (2026-09-27): concepts that say much the
  same thing under different titles and tags. The mechanical pass (same
  title) and the eve screen (shared tags, overlapping titles) can't see
  these;
- the concepts behind a question that found no answer (2026-09-27, above).

Search stays library science: a controlled vocabulary, cross-references,
and review dates, with Jev judging relevance where it matters.

**How concepts are embedded** (`convex/similar.ts`):
- **The text:** a concept is a document: its title, description, and the
  first 2,000 characters of its body. Qwen3 puts its instruction on the
  query side only. A question looked up against concepts is embedded with
  a retrieval instruction; a question compared with other questions, with
  its own.
- **Storage:** one 256-dimension vector per concept. It's embedded again
  when the concept changes, and deleted with it.
- **Runs:** at most 512 concepts a run. A big library is embedded over
  several runs, and the first backfill costs well under a cent per
  thousand concepts.
- **"Near" means:** cosine 0.75 between two concepts, and 0.45 between a
  question and a concept. Past that, Jev decides.
- **Checking it:** `npx convex run embeddings:probe` makes a real call and
  shows where a duplicate, a related concept, an unrelated one, and a
  question's answer land.

**The models, as the Vercel AI Gateway listed them on 2026-09-25:**

| Model | Price per million tokens | Zero data retention | Trains on requests | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `alibaba/qwen3-embedding-8b` | $0.01 | yes, every provider (DeepInfra, Nebius) | no | **The model, since 2026-09-26**, pinned to DeepInfra (US). Open weights, 32k context, Matryoshka, top-tier |
| `google/gemini-embedding-001` | $0.15 | yes, on Vertex AI (US) | no | The first default (2026-09-25). A US model, top-tier, at 15× the price |
| `perplexity/pplx-embed-v1-0.6b` | $0.004 | no | no | The cheapest, US. Not chosen: no provider offers zero retention |
| `google/gemini-embedding-2` | $0.20 | no (Google's Gemini API only) | no | Not chosen: its strength is images, audio, and video, which librocat does not have, at 20× Qwen's price. It is no-training, but not zero-retention, so Google may keep request logs for a time |
| `amazon/titan-embed-text-v2`, `google/text-embedding-005` | $0.02–0.025 | yes | no | US, cheaper, weaker |

**Why Qwen3-Embedding-8B on DeepInfra:** inference in the US, zero
retention required on every request, no training, top-tier quality, and
the lowest price of any zero-retention model.
- The lab is Alibaba, but only its open weights are used. DeepInfra runs
  them in its own US data centers, and no request reaches Alibaba.
- The gateway request is pinned (`only: ["deepinfra"]`). That keeps it off
  Nebius, which also runs in the EU.
- If DeepInfra is down, questions group by their words until it's back.
- Merges are Jev's call: the embedding only proposes the nearest earlier
  questions.

**What would widen their use:** search ranking, and only after the
retrieval harness (`packages/core/tests/retrieval.test.ts`) and real
libraries show it helps. Local librocat stays offline, with no embeddings.

concepts.title: Local and hosted, together
concepts.description: The CLI moves a library between the two, the way `supabase db push/pull` moves a schema: ```bash librocat login # sign in to the hosted library (browser, OAuth) librocat push [dir] # this folder's OKF files -> the hosted library librocat pu
concepts.body:
The CLI moves a library between the two, the way `supabase db push/pull`
moves a schema:

```bash
librocat login          # sign in to the hosted library (browser, OAuth)
librocat push [dir]     # this folder's OKF files -> the hosted library
librocat pull [dir]     # the hosted library -> OKF files here, e.g. to commit
librocat whoami
librocat logout
```

After a commit, `librocat changed` puts the concepts whose `sources` name a
file it touched up for review (their review date becomes now). With
`--remote` it does the same in the hosted library, and `--since ORIG_HEAD`
covers a pull or merge. As a hook: `echo 'npx librocat changed' >>
.git/hooks/post-commit`.

`librocat login` offers to push a local library into a brand-new, empty
hosted one, and never touches a library that already holds concepts.
`librocat mcp --remote` serves the hosted library on stdio, for an agent that
cannot connect to a remote MCP server itself; its `ingest_repo` still reads
this machine's disk.

concepts.title: Workflow
concepts.description: - Commit the OKF files to your own Git repo (GitHub, GitLab, or anywhere).
concepts.body:
- Commit the OKF files to your own Git repo (GitHub, GitLab, or anywhere).
  The repo is the source of truth, not the index and not librocat.
- The MCP tools are the only read/write interface. See
  [mcp-tools.md](./mcp-tools.md).
- **Your agent is the indexer.** When it ingests a concept it writes the
  title, description, and tags itself. `ingest_repo` writes a mechanical
  description, and your agent improves it with `update`. (The hosted
  library catalogs what the writer left blank, and Libro keeps it in order.)
- The index rebuilds from the files at every launch. After you edit files
  outside the MCP (an editor, a `git pull`), ask your agent to run `reindex`.
- `status` reports `stale: true` when the files on disk and the index disagree.
- `history` is the file's Git log (keep the bundle inside a Git repo);
  `weed_report` lists what to review; `thesaurus` is the tag vocabulary (one
  concept file, `thesaurus.md`); `finding_aid` with `write: true` writes an
  `index.md` shelf list into each directory.
- There is nothing to persist except the files.

concepts.title: Self-hosting the full service
concepts.description: `librocat start` is the library, not the hosted service.
concepts.body:
`librocat start` is the library, not the hosted service. The hosted service
(dashboard, sign-in, teams, Libro) is this repository's `apps/web` on Convex
and Vercel; running all of it yourself is documented in DEVELOPERS.md. Set
`LIBROCAT_SELF_HOST=1` on both the Convex deployment and the Next.js app:
no plans, no quotas, and no Billing page.

concepts.title: Notes
concepts.description: - **Shelves.
concepts.body:
- **Shelves.** `search` and `list` take `shelf` (the leading directory of
  concept ids, `"acme"` for `acme/...`): one library, many shelves. A project
  reads its own shelf first and the whole library second. Split a library
  only when access must differ (docs/okf.md §Shelves).
- **Several libraries (hosted).** The MCP URL picks one: `/mcp` is your
  default library, and `/mcp?library=<slug>` another you belong to (the
  dashboard shows each library's URL; the CLI takes `--library`). `status`
  says which library this is (`library`) and lists the others
  (`libraries`). See docs/cloud.md §Several libraries.

- **Author entry** (Cutter's object D). `search` and `list` take `author`:
  only concepts that writer wrote. Hosted, that is everyone who wrote a
  revision (the cataloger aside): a member by email (or `human:<email>`),
  `me`, an agent by its name (`Claude Code`), or `process:libro`.
  `get_concept` lists them as `authors`, people by email. Local reads the
  Git log instead: a commit author's name or email, or `me` (the repo's
  configured user); uncommitted writes have no author yet, and a bundle
  outside Git says so.
- **Writes** (`ingest`, `update`, `rename`, `delete`, `ingest_repo`) edit OKF
  files (Local) or Convex rows (Cloud) and update the index in the same call.
  In Cloud every write also appends a revision.
- **`history`** is Git history in Local (the bundle must live inside a Git
  repository; `revision` is a commit hash) and the revisions table in Cloud
  (`revision` is the sequence number). Both return the same shape:
  `revisions[]` newest first, or `snapshot` with `frontmatter` and `body`.
- **`delete`** removes one concept. Links from other concepts to it become
  broken links (`status` counts them) until you fix or remove them.
- **Ids are never reused by default** (a library's accession numbers,
  Dana, ch. XIX). A deleted id, and the old id of a renamed concept, are
  retired: `ingest` never derives one again (it bumps to `-2`), and reading
  one says what became of it (`concept not found: x (deleted on 2026-09-20
  ("Title"))`, or `(renamed to y on …)`). An explicit `id` may still take a
  retired id; the result says so in `reused`. Local keeps them in the
  bundle's `log.md` (OKF's update log); hosted keeps them per workspace and
  writes the same `log.md` into the export.
- **Supersession.** `update` with `superseded_by` retires a concept in favor
  of another (a "see" reference): status becomes `deprecated` unless given,
  `get_concept` and `search` return `superseded_by`, and `search` sinks
  deprecated hits below live ones unless you filter on `status`.
- **Thesaurus.** The controlled vocabulary lives in one concept (`thesaurus`,
  type `Thesaurus`, `terms` in frontmatter), shaped like a library thesaurus
  (ANSI/NISO Z39.19): broader (BT), narrower (NT), related (RT, "see also"),
  and use-for (UF) terms, plus a scope note (SN) per tag. Writes map
  `use_for` synonyms onto the preferred tag; `search` expands a preferred
  tag with its narrower terms and a synonym with its preferred tag; a `tag`
  filter on `search` or `list` includes every narrower term below the tag.
  Hosted cataloging reads scope notes when it picks tags, and files under
  the most specific tag (a broader tag goes when a narrower one applies).
- **The ready-reference file (hosted).** Every `search` is filed as a
  question, with what it found and the concept the agent opens next (its
  answer). Asked again, the question gets that answer as its first hit,
  marked `ready_reference: true`. What found no answer shows on the
  dashboard's reference desk and in Libro's weekly report. Questions are
  kept 90 days; one that looks like it carries a secret is never kept.
- **Review dates.** `stale_after` (OKF's lifecycle field) is when a concept
  should be checked again: an ISO date such as `2026-12-31`, set on anything
  time-bound (a plan, a price, a version, an owner). Every summary in
  `search`, `list`, and `get_concept` ca

concepts.title: Ids and paths
concepts.description: The concept id is the file's bundle path without `.
concepts.body:
The concept id is the file's bundle path without `.md`. librocat appends `.md` when
writing, so ids that contain dots round-trip (a Python file `code/index.py` is
stored at `code/index.py.md` and keeps the id `code/index.py`).

concepts.title: Shelves: one library, many projects
concepts.description: The leading directory of an id is its **shelf** (`acme/auth-flow` sits on the `acme` shelf).
concepts.body:
The leading directory of an id is its **shelf** (`acme/auth-flow` sits on the
`acme` shelf). A library stays one connected whole (one thesaurus, one graph,
one weeding report), and projects are shelves in it. `search` and `list`
take `shelf: "acme"` to scope a read to one project, and an agent working in
that project searches its shelf first and the whole library second. Every
shelf gets its own finding aid (`index.md`). Do not split a library into
several to get per-project views; that is what a shelf is for. Split only
when access must differ (a client under NDA, personal vs employer): that is
a second library (hosted: its own `?library=` URL) or a second repo (Local).

concepts.title: Links become the graph
concepts.description: Only Markdown links to `.
concepts.body:
Only Markdown links to `.md` targets become graph edges:

- `/path/from/bundle.md` — bundle-relative
- `./sibling.md`, `../up.md` — relative to the concept

External URLs and anchors are ignored. `neighbors` and `graph` see exactly the
links you write, so link generously.

concepts.title: Reserved files
concepts.description: `index.
concepts.body:
`index.md` and `log.md` are reserved (directory listing and update log). They are
not indexed as concepts. librocat writes the bundle-root `log.md` when a concept
is deleted or renamed, under date headings, newest first:

```markdown

concepts.description: * **Deletion**: `notes/old` — Old title * **Rename**: `notes/a` → `notes/b` ``` It reads the log back, so a retired id is never handed to a new concept by default.
concepts.body:
* **Deletion**: `notes/old` — Old title
* **Rename**: `notes/a` → `notes/b`
```

It reads the log back, so a retired id is never handed to a new concept by
default. Anything else in the log is kept.

concepts.title: Dublin Core, roughly
concepts.description: OKF frontmatter maps nearly one-to-one onto [Dublin Core](https://www.
concepts.body:
OKF frontmatter maps nearly one-to-one onto [Dublin Core](https://www.dublincore.org/specifications/dublin-core/dces/),
the fifteen-element library metadata standard: `title` → dc:title,
`description` → dc:description, `tags` → dc:subject, `type` → dc:type, links →
dc:relation. The format is a hand-authorable catalog record, not an invented
schema. (The one element OKF lacks is dc:date — Git history holds it in Local; Cloud stamps `created_at`/`updated_at` and keeps a revision per write.)

concepts.title: Standards and references
concepts.description: The specs librocat implements and the references it follows.
concepts.body:
The specs librocat implements and the references it follows. When one of
these changes, the code follows it, not the other way around.

| Reference | What it governs in librocat |
| --- | --- |
| [Agent Plugins](https://agent-plugins.org/) | The plugin layout (`plugin.json`, `mcp.json`, `skills/`). Remote servers are `"type": "streamable-http"` with a `url`; OAuth is the host's job, and headers must never carry secrets |
| [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io/home) | The `SKILL.md` format of the skills in the plugin, and the `npx skills add librocat/librocat` path for agents without Agent Plugin support |
| [MCP TypeScript SDK](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk) | The server and client SDK (v2) behind every MCP surface: the remote `/mcp`, the local server, the CLI bridge, the e2e clients |
| [mcp-handler](https://github.com/vercel-labs/mcp-handler) | The remote MCP route on Vercel: stateless Streamable HTTP, `withMcpAuth` (401 + RFC 9728 challenge), the protected-resource metadata |
| [Open Knowledge Format, the announcement](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/data-analytics/how-the-open-knowledge-format-can-improve-data-sharing) | Why OKF exists: a shared Markdown library that agents read and update, curated like code |
| [OKF SPEC](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/knowledge-catalog/blob/main/okf/SPEC.md) | The storage and export format: frontmatter (`type` required), bundles, `index.md` / `log.md`, links, provenance (`generated`, `verified`, `sources`, `stale_after`) |
| [LLM Wiki (Karpathy)](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f) | The pattern librocat productizes: an LLM-maintained wiki with ingest, query, and lint. In librocat: `ingest`, `search`, `weed_report`, and Libro |

concepts.title: The idea: Libro in a badge, drawn in one line (the Yarn direction)
concepts.description: librocat = *libro* (book) + *cat*, and the cat has a name: **Libro, the library cat**, librocat's librarian.
concepts.body:
librocat = *libro* (book) + *cat*, and the cat has a name: **Libro, the
library cat**, librocat's librarian. The mark follows the **Yarn logo**: a
solid **rounded square** (the same corner feel as the site's cards), and
inside it the cat drawn as a **single monoline outline** in
one light color, one continuous stroke, hand-drawn but simple. Two
differences from Yarn: Yarn's cat has its back to us; **Libro faces the
viewer** (three-quarter front), sitting up and attentive, the way a
librarian faces the desk. And **Libro sits on a closed book**, drawn in the
same line. No hat. Because Libro faces
us, the head gets a small, friendly face drawn in the same line as
everything else: **two happy closed eyes** (short arcs curving upward, the
way a cat's eyes go when it purrs) behind **small round glasses**, a **tiny
nose**, a **small w-shaped mouth** under it, and **three short whiskers on
each cheek**. Nothing filled: a filled dot
inside an outlined head is what makes a monoline face look off. Libro is a
**kitten**: baby proportions (big head, big ears, small body, big paws),
cute and friendly the way Yarn's cat is, and the glasses make the kitten a
librarian: smart, sitting up straight, on the book. Kitten plus glasses is
the whole character in one glance.

Why this works: the badge scales from favicon to hero without changing
(the full drawing above 32 px, the head crop below, both the same line),
it is warm and friendly without becoming a full cartoon (no fills, no
color inside the face, one line weight), and one continuous stroke is a
signature nobody else has (Yarn's is a beanie; ours is the book). It also
gives Libro a face the copy can point at ("Libro pulled 4 concepts for
review").

concepts.title: The favicon: Libro's head as a silhouette, from the same drawing (decided 2026-08-25)
concepts.description: A full cat-on-book in a 16 px tile is about 10 px of cat: it muddies no matter how it is rendered (a solid silhouette of the *whole cat* was tried and dropped).
concepts.body:
A full cat-on-book in a 16 px tile is about 10 px of cat: it muddies no
matter how it is rendered (a solid silhouette of the *whole cat* was tried
and dropped). The favicon is therefore **the head only**, the standard
mascot-favicon move: the head is where all the cute lives, and head +
ears + glasses fills the whole tile with shapes big enough to survive
16 px. And at 16 px even the thickened line head is a smudge (1 px lines
on a green field; tested in a Chrome tab strip on 2026-08-25), so the
head mark is the head **as a plain silhouette, the GitHub move**: the head
outline filled, whiskers, glasses, and eyes dropped (the glasses are
dropped too: two cut-out discs muddied the 16 px tile, and the Octocat
proves a plain silhouette is enough), in **green on a paper rounded
square** with the badge's corner radius, filling the whole tile, no
sticker border. `scripts/trace-logo.py` derives it from the traced head
(`public/logo-head.svg`); it is not a separate generation and needs no
prompt of its own. It is one file everywhere below the hero: the 28 px
lockups (header, footer, auth pages, dashboard, where the line head was
gray noise) and the browser tab (`apps/web/src/app/icon.svg` is a copy;
`favicon.ico` and `apple-icon.png` are rasterized from it), so the tab
icon and the header mark are the same image. On the site's paper
background the square melts away and the green head sits next to the
wordmark, the way the Octocat sits in GitHub's header; on a dark tab strip
the paper square pops.

How the line mark becomes the head mark:

- **Crop, do not redraw.** Take the traced line mark and keep the head:
  the head outline, both ears with the notch between them, the glasses
  rings with the bridge, the happy closed eyes inside them, and the
  whiskers. Delete the body, paws, tail, book, temple, nose, and mouth. Same geometry,
  never a second generation.
- **Enlarge and fill.** Scale the head to about 0.8 of the tile's side
  and fill the outline in green, so the shape holds at 16 and 28 px.
  Center it optically (a touch below center, balanced under the ears).
- **Plain.** The glasses, the eyes, and the whiskers belong to the line
  mark (the hero). The head mark is the outline only: ears, cheeks, the
  tuft. What makes it Libro at that size is the shape and the green.
- **Same shape, no sticker.** The head mark's ground is a paper rounded
  square with the badge's corner radius, filling the tile with no sticker
  border, so it rhymes with the hero badge and the site's cards without
  wasting tile.

Coherence check, in one glance: the favicon must look like a zoom into
the hero mark's head, the same head at the same angle. If the head needs redrawing to read at 16 px, fix the traced
line mark's head and let both crops inherit it.

concepts.title: Fit with the site
concepts.description: The mark must look like it was drawn by the same hand as the website (`apps/web`): paper background, ink text, one green accent, IBM Plex Mono wordmark, hairline borders, cards with a soft radius, a faint ruled "catalog card" behind the her
concepts.body:
The mark must look like it was drawn by the same hand as the website
(`apps/web`): paper background, ink text, one green accent, IBM Plex Mono
wordmark, hairline borders, cards with a soft radius, a faint ruled
"catalog card" behind the hero. Rules that keep the mark in that world:

- **Colors only from the site tokens.** Green `#1F744F` badge, paper
  `#F9FAFC` line, or ink `#141B26` where the badge is ink. The only other
  mark on the page is the line mark's hairline sticker edge, ink at 12 %
  opacity, on both crops. No blush, no highlight,
  no gradient. On the dark theme the badge stays green and the line stays
  paper.
- **Line weight like the site's rules.** The site's borders are 1 px
  hairlines; the line mark's stroke is about 1/24 of the side (about 2.5 px
  at the 56 px small-screen hero, 10 px at the 240 px hero). Round caps, the
  way the site's rounded corners feel. At 32 px and below the head mark
  takes over, with its stroke thickened to about 1/12 of the side.
- **Flat, calm, no effects.** No shadow, no bevel. The only edge is the
  sticker's paper border with its hairline, which is what lets the badge sit
  on the ruled catalog card like a sticker on a notebook page. The rounded
  square is the same shape family as every card on the site.
- **Cute, but in the site's register.** The site is plain and composed
  (Hormozi copy, book-face headings). Libro's cuteness comes from
  proportion and the happy eyes, not from stickers: no sparkles, no hearts,
  no speech bubbles, no paw prints around the badge.
- **Sits with the wordmark.** In the header the badge is 20 px next to
  `librocat` in Plex Mono, so at that size it must read as "cat in a
  rounded square" and nothing more. Use the head mark there, as in the
  favicon; the full line mark starts above 32 px.

concepts.title: Geometry
concepts.description: - **Badge, as a sticker**: a solid green **rounded square** with a corner radius of about 20 % of the side (the proportion of the site's `rounded-xl` cards; app-icon shape, not a circle), and around it a paper border about 4 % of the side w
concepts.body:
- **Badge, as a sticker**: a solid green **rounded square** with a corner
  radius of about 20 % of the side (the proportion of the site's `rounded-xl`
  cards; app-icon shape, not a circle), and around it a paper border about
  4 % of the side wide, cut like a die-cut sticker (following the rounded
  square), with a hairline edge in ink at about 12 % opacity so the paper
  border shows on the site's paper background. Whole sticker fills the
  canvas with about 4 % margin. This is what makes the mark sit on the
  hero's ruled catalog card like a sticker on a notebook page. The sticker
  border and hairline are part of the badge in both crops: the head mark
  (20 px lockups, favicon, app icon) keeps them too, collapsing at tiny
  sizes.
- **Line**: a **green cat, never a white cat**. The paper line only draws
  Libro's outline and the badge's green shows through inside it: nothing
  is ever filled in the line mark. The head mark is the one exception: a
  green silhouette on paper (see The favicon), because at 16 and 28 px a
  line cannot be seen. Everything inside the badge is one stroke weight, about 1/24 of
  the badge's side, round caps and joins, in the light color. No fills
  inside the badge except the badge itself and the head mark's silhouette. The cat should read as one
  continuous line where possible (back, head, ear, ear, head, chest, front
  paw, book, tail), the way Yarn's does; the face and the whiskers are
  the short separate strokes, same weight.
- **Pose and proportions (kitten)**: Libro sits upright with the **body
  in three-quarter view turned to the viewer's left** (chest and front
  paws angled toward the left edge of the badge, haunch on the right) and
  the **head turned to the viewer**, smiling straight at them, the way a
  kitten turns its head when called. Both ears show; the chest line and
  both front paws are visible. The body direction is not optional: in the
  hero the mark sits right of the headline, so Libro's body leans toward
  the text while the face greets the reader. Body never turned right,
  never dead front; face never in profile. Baby proportions: the
  head is about half the whole cat's height, round, with chubby cheeks
  and big ears (each about 0.2 of the side, tips softly rounded, set
  wide); the body is tiny and round under it, on short stubby legs; paws
  oversized for the body; the tail short. Chibi, never adult. Whole kitten
  about 0.6 of the side tall, centered slightly right; the short tail is
  held straight up behind the haunch, the way a happy cat carries it, with
  the tip curling forward in a soft hook (a question mark), never lying on
  the book or wrapped around the base. Friendly and upright: back
  straight, head level.
- **The book**: under Libro, a closed hardcover in a light three-quarter
  view from above and from the left (the chosen generation, 2026-08-23),
  about 0.55 of the side wide and 0.15 tall with its thickness, drawn in
  the same line: the top cover as a flat parallelogram with rounded
  corners, the fore-edge facing front-left as a band with three parallel
  page lines, the rounded spine on the right with two lines along it. It
  must read as a book on its own, not as a plinth. It sits flat; Libro's
  weight rests on the cover; the tail rises from the right side of the
  body, above the spine side of the book, and never touches or crosses
  the book.
- **Face**: small round glasses, two rings each about 0.1 of the side
  across (the head is about 0.3 of the side across, so the two rings plus
  a one-stroke bridge sit inside it with a margin), joined by a short bridge, drawn in the same stroke (no temples
  needed at three quarters, or one short temple to the near ear); inside
  each ring a happy closed eye, a short arc curving upward (like ^ ^, a
  purring cat); one tiny nose (a small rounded v) under the bridge; a small
  w-shaped mouth just below it; **three short whiskers on each cheek**,
  straight, fanning out slightly from beside the mouth,

concepts.title: Lockups
concepts.description: - **Horizontal**: mark, then a gap of 0.
concepts.body:
- **Horizontal**: mark, then a gap of 0.4 × the mark's width (8 px at 20 px), then the wordmark
  `librocat` in a monospace face (IBM Plex Mono in the site), lowercase,
  `libro` in ink and `cat` in green. The wordmark's x-height centers on the
  badge's center.
- **Stacked**: mark above the wordmark, centered, gap of 0.35 × mark height.
- **Hero**: the mark alone, large, in the right two fifths of the landing
  page's ruled catalog card, with the headline, lead, install command, and
  buttons in the left three fifths (text left so it is read first, the mark
  as the reward at the end of the line). No wordmark under it (the wordmark
  is in the header). Sized to the visual weight of the headline block, about
  240 px. On small screens the split collapses: the mark on top at 56 px,
  text below. This is the one place the mark stands by itself, so the
  drawing must read as a cat on a book with no help from the name.
- **Favicon / app icon**: the head-mark badge itself is the icon, in the
  same sticker format as the hero (green rounded square, sticker border,
  hairline), no wordmark, no extra padding. The app icon at 192 and
  512 px is the same head mark, so the icon is one image at every size.

concepts.body:
Order: generate the line mark first (2048 × 2048), pick the winner, then
run the favicon prompt on that image as an edit, so the favicon is the
same face in the same sticker. The shipped favicon.ico is still built
from the traced SVG (From PNG to SVG, step 4); the favicon generation
previews the look and serves as the tracing reference for the head. Grok
Imagine has no negative-prompt field, so the exclusions are inside the
prompts. Judge generations on the drawing, not the exact tint: the hex
values are set when tracing.

Whiskers, in both renderings: three short straight strokes on each
cheek, fanning out from beside the mouth, the same weight and round caps
as the line. They are the one departure from the single continuous
stroke, so keep them short and few (never long, never curved, never
more than three a side) so they read at 20 px; at 16 px they go with the
eye arcs.

> an adult cat: chibi proportions with a huge round head about as big as

concepts.title: From PNG to SVG
concepts.description: `python3 scripts/trace-logo.
concepts.body: `python3 scripts/trace-logo.py ` does all of this in one go (page dropped, sticker and badge redrawn as exact rounded rects in the site's hex, the paper line traced with potrace, the head stroke the head silhouette filled, favicon set rasterized). The manual route, for reference: 1. Pick the cleanest generation; crop to the square with margin. 2. Trace: `potrace` (via Inkscape → Path → Trace Bitmap, single scan, threshold ~0.5) or `vtracer` (mode: polygon off, spline on). Better for a monoline: retrace the line by hand in Inkscape or Figma as one stroked path (round caps), then Stroke to Path, so the weight stays exact. 3. Simplify the path (Inkscape: Path → Simplify at 0.002) until the SVG is one `` under about 2 KB. 4. Make the head mark from the traced line mark, not from a separate generation: duplicate the traced drawing, delete everything but the head (head outline, ears, glasses rings and bridge, eye arcs, whiskers), scale the head to about 0.7 of the badge's side, thicken the stroke to about 1/12 of the side (increase the stroke width before Stroke to Path), and center it on the same sticker badge as the hero (green rounded square, sticker border, hairline). Keep a copy with the eye arcs and whiskers (32 px and up) and one without (16 px) only if they muddy; otherwise one file. 5. Export `logo.svg` (the line-mark badge, above 32 px) and `logo-head.svg` (the head-mark badge, 32 px and below) into `apps/web/public/`. No lockup file: the wordmark is code (`brand.tsx`), and the OG image composes the line mark and the wordmark in code. 6. Wire it in: `LogoMark` in `apps/web/src/components/brand.tsx` is an `` of `logo-head.svg`, or `logo.svg` with the `line` prop (the hero's `size-60` and `size-14`). The badge carries its own two colors, so it does not need `currentColor`; keep the badge green in both themes and let the line stay paper. The favicon set in `apps/web/src/app/` comes from `logo-head.svg`: `favicon.ico` (16, 32, 48), `icon.svg` (a copy), and `apple-icon.png` (180, flattened on paper: iOS paints transparency black), all three from `logo-head.svg` (`icon.svg` is a copy). `opengraph-image.tsx` composes the OG card from `logo.svg`.

concepts.title: Start
concepts.description: You need Docker with Compose v2, or Podman with `podman compose`.
concepts.body:
You need Docker with Compose v2, or Podman with `podman compose`. You also
need git, openssl, and about 2 GB of memory.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/librocat/librocat.git
cd librocat/self-host
./setup.sh          # with Podman: COMPOSE="podman compose" ./setup.sh
```

`setup.sh` does the following, and is safe to run again:
1. writes the secrets to `self-host/.env`;
2. starts Convex and takes its admin key;
3. builds the image;
4. deploys the functions;
5. starts the site.

The first build takes a few minutes. Keep `.env`: it's the key to your data.

Then:

1. **Open http://localhost:3000 and create an account.** No email service is
   set up yet, so the verification code goes to the function log. Run
   `./logs.sh --history 100` and look for "verification code".
2. **Connect an agent** to `http://localhost:3000/mcp`. For example:

   ```bash
   claude mcp add --transport http librocat http://localhost:3000/mcp
   ```

   On its first call, the agent opens your browser to sign in and approve
   it. Use `localhost`, not `127.0.0.1`: the address is part of every token.

concepts.title: Settings
concepts.description: Set these in `self-host/.
concepts.body:
Set these in `self-host/.env`, then apply them with `docker compose up -d
--build`.

| Variable | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `AUTH_RESEND_KEY` | Email sign-up and password codes through [Resend](https://resend.com). Unset: codes go to the log. |
| `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` | Automatic cataloging by Jev, and Libro's screens after each review: review dates, duplicates by meaning, and the concepts behind unanswered questions (Jev and Qwen3 embeddings), all through the Vercel AI Gateway. Unset: no model is called. |
| `LIBROCAT_PORT` | The site's port on this machine (default 3000). |
| `LIBROCAT_SITE_URL` | The address people and agents use (default `http://localhost:$LIBROCAT_PORT`). |
| `CONVEX_CLOUD_ORIGIN`, `CONVEX_SITE_ORIGIN` | Where browsers reach Convex (default `http://127.0.0.1:3210` and `:3211`). |
| `LIBROCAT_BIND` | The interface the ports are published on (default `127.0.0.1`). |

concepts.title: On a server, with a domain
concepts.description: Put a reverse proxy with TLS in front, such as Caddy or nginx on the same host.
concepts.body:
Put a reverse proxy with TLS in front, such as Caddy or nginx on the same
host. It needs three names:
- the site, to port 3000;
- Convex, to port 3210;
- Convex's HTTP actions, to port 3211.

For example, in `.env`:

```bash
LIBROCAT_SITE_URL=https://kb.example.com
CONVEX_CLOUD_ORIGIN=https://convex.kb.example.com
CONVEX_SITE_ORIGIN=https://auth.kb.example.com
```

Then run `docker compose up -d --build`; the addresses are built into the
site.

The site's server reaches Convex at those same public addresses, so the
server must be able to resolve them.

Anyone who can reach the site can create an account and a library of their
own. People join a shared library through a Team invite link. If you don't
want open sign-up, keep the site on a private network, or put your proxy's
own login in front of it.

concepts.title: Run it
concepts.body:
- **Logs:**
  - `./logs.sh` for the Convex functions (Ctrl+C to stop);
  - `docker compose logs web` for the site.
- **Convex's dashboard:** run `docker compose --profile admin up -d`, then
  open http://localhost:6791 and paste `CONVEX_ADMIN_KEY` from `.env`.
- **Backups:** everything lives in the `convex-data` volume. To take a
  snapshot:

  ```bash
  docker compose run --rm --no-deps -v "$PWD/backups:/backups" deploy \
    sh -c 'cd apps/web && node_modules/.bin/convex export --path /backups/librocat.zip'
  ```

  `convex import` restores one. The dashboard's Export also gives each
  library as plain OKF files, which work with `npx librocat start`.
- **Upgrade:** `git pull && docker compose up -d --build`. The deploy step
  pushes the new functions.
- **Stop:**
  - `docker compose down` keeps the data;
  - `docker compose down -v` deletes it.

concepts.title: How it differs from librocat.dev
concepts.description: - There is no billing and there are no quotas.
concepts.body:

- Convex runs on SQLite in the volume. For Postgres, S3, or several
  machines, see [Convex's self-hosting guide](https://github.com/get-convex/convex-backend/tree/main/self-hosted)
  and add its settings to the `convex` service.

concepts.description: The Convex deployment starts a session here after each weekly review (or "Ask Libro now"): "Review workspace `<id>`".
concepts.body:
The Convex deployment starts a session here after each weekly review (or
"Ask Libro now"): "Review workspace `<id>`". Libro reads the review shelf,
the weeding report, the thesaurus, and the concepts that matter, then files
proposals on the same review shelf a human sees on the dashboard: `merge`
(with a drafted merged concept), `supersede`, `deprecate`, `synonym`. Libro
proposes, the user disposes. Nothing changes until someone clicks Approve.

Tools (`agent/tools/`): `status`, `review_shelf`, `weed_report`, `thesaurus`,
`search`, `list`, `get_concept`, `neighbors`, `propose`. Reads and the propose
call go to two service routes on the Convex deployment (`/libro/read`,
`/libro/propose`, see `apps/web/convex/http.ts`) with a shared bearer secret.

review:

```bash

cannot connect to a remote MCP server itself.

concepts.title: What we store
concepts.description: Laughing Hermit, Inc.
concepts.body: Laughing Hermit, Inc. operates librocat and is the data controller. We store your account email, your workspace's concepts (the knowledge you and your agents write), the derived index (search text, and one embedding per concept), a revision per write, Libro's review-shelf proposals, usage counters (concept retrievals and index credits), and the ready-reference file: the questions your agents ask the library (search queries), what they found, and which concept answered them, so a question asked again gets its answer first and Libro can report what found no answer. A query that looks like it carries a secret is never kept. Billing runs through Stripe. We never see or store card numbers.

concepts.title: What we do not do
concepts.description: We do not sell your data.
concepts.body: We do not sell your data. We do not train models on your concepts. Automatic cataloging sends only the concept being described (title, type, body) and your workspace's tag names to a model, and stores only the result in your workspace. Before Libro's weekly review, only the titles, descriptions, and tags of concepts that may be duplicates are sent. After it, Jev reads the concepts written or changed since it last looked (title, description, and the start of the body, up to 20 a review) to suggest a review date for what is tied to a date. Jev also judges pairs an embedding proposes: concepts that may say the same thing (up to 20 pairs a review), and the concepts a question that found no answer is about (up to 10 questions a review), from their titles, descriptions, tags, and the start of their bodies. On paid plans, Libro, the library cat, then reads the concepts it reviews with a model. These requests go through Vercel's AI Gateway, only to models whose providers do not train on them, and the generative ones (Gemini, and Libro's own model) ask for zero data retention. Embeddings come from Qwen3-Embedding, an open model that DeepInfra runs in the US with zero data retention (nothing is sent to its maker, Alibaba). Each question's text is embedded to group rewordings, and each concept's title, description, and the start of its body to find duplicates and the concepts behind unanswered questions. One vector per distinct question and one per concept are kept, and each is deleted with its question or concept.
